title: Commentary on the Mishnah
hookLine: written in Arabic while he was still young and wandering

lines: WRITTEN ON THE ROAD AND AT SEA.
cards: A long book, and at the very end of it, an apology. Maimonides closes one of his early books by asking the reader for patience.
He wrote it, he says, while his mind was troubled and while he was on the move, some of it on the road and some of it at sea. So if you find a mistake, he asks, judge him kindly.

Then look at what he had taken on while traveling: the Mishnah, the core text of the oral law, explained passage by passage. He says he wrote it while he was still young. Today, the book that started him.

teach.h: WRITTEN IN ARABIC, IN HEBREW LETTERS.
teach.b: Commentary on the Mishnah. In Hebrew, Perush HaMishnayot. First, the language.
Maimonides wrote it in Arabic, the everyday language of the Jews around him, set down in Hebrew letters. He wanted it read and used, not admired.
Hebrew translations came later, and those are what readers of the Hebrew page meet today. Second, the method. The Mishnah is terse.
It often starts in the middle of an argument, as if you already know what the argument is about.
Maimonides goes passage by passage and asks the beginner's questions. What is this about? What does this word mean?
Which view is the law? Then he gives the bottom line, plainly. Third, the doorways.
Before some sections he wrote long introductions that read like books of their own. One opens the whole Mishnah and explains how the oral tradition was handed down.

One, on a chapter of tractate Sanhedrin, sets out the foundations of Jewish belief. One, before Pirkei Avot, is about the health of the soul. In the days ahead we'll walk through two of those doorways.
Fourth, the ambition. A young man without a settled home decides to explain the whole Mishnah to ordinary readers, in their own language. And on the last page he asks forgiveness for his mistakes.
Ambition and humility, bound into one book.

how: Students of the Mishnah often read Maimonides' commentary, in Hebrew translation, alongside the text; his introductions, such as the one to Pirkei Avot, are also studied on their own.

games.q: what does “commentary on the mishnah” mean?
o: the Talmud's own line-by-line discussion of the Mishnah
Rashi's notes printed in the Mishnah's inner margin
Maimonides' early book explaining each Mishnah passage

games.q: the commentary on the Mishnah — tap the pairs.

s: Maimonides wrote his commentary on the Mishnah in Hebrew
he wrote it in Arabic, in Hebrew letters; Hebrew translations came later.
he says he wrote some of it on the road and at sea
he says so at the end, and asks the reader to judge his mistakes kindly.
the commentary only gives rulings, with no introductions
before some sections he wrote long introductions, including one on the foundations of belief.

games.q: you're a young scholar on the move, with no settled home. you want to explain the Mishnah to ordinary readers. what do you do?
o: wait until life is settled and quiet.
begin now, on the road, in the language people speak.
write only for scholars, in the hardest style you know.
games.why: Maimonides begins on the move, writes in Arabic so people can use it, and apologizes at the end for any mistakes.

practice: Bring to mind something you've meant to do for a long time: a book to read, a text to study, a letter that will need many versions. Don't plan all of it; picture only the first step, small enough to be real.
Maimonides didn't wait for a quiet room or a settled life.
